missing_spec_content.spec_text: explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only states the trends: "Trends: coal use is falling. The use of renewable resources is rising." (keyPoints[2].content). It never explains why, for example concern about CO₂ and climate change, emissions targets and legislation, the falling cost of wind and solar, or fossil fuels running out. The specification asks students to explain the trends, not just describe them.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: compare ways that different energy resources are used, the uses to include transport, electricity generation and heating
missing_spec_content.why: Transport and heating get one sentence each: "For example, petrol and diesel fuel cars. Gas heats many homes." (keyPoints[2].content). Nothing compares how different resources are used for each purpose, for example bio-fuel or electricity for transport, or electric, solar or geothermal heating. The table compares resources only "for the national grid", which is electricity generation.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson's definition, "A renewable resource is one that is replenished as it is used." (keyPoints[2].content), drops the "(or can be)" part. That part is what makes bio-fuel count as renewable. Its absence may explain why the table marks bio-fuel only "Potentially" renewable.

factual_errors.text: It could come from a wind farm off Scotland or a nuclear power station in Somerset.
factual_errors.correction: Somerset's only operating nuclear power station, Hinkley Point B, stopped generating in 2022. Hinkley Point C is still being built. Electricity cannot currently come from a nuclear power station in Somerset.

factual_errors.text: Coal: the most CO₂ per kWh and the cheapest to burn. It is being phased out.
factual_errors.correction: The UK's last coal-fired power station (Ratcliffe-on-Soar) closed in 2024, so coal has already been phased out of UK electricity generation. "Cheapest to burn" is also doubtful once carbon costs are included. At most, coal fuel is relatively cheap.

factual_errors.text: tidal: very predictable, because tides never stop.
factual_errors.correction: Tidal power is predictable because tides follow a regular, known cycle. The reason is not that they "never stop". There are periods of slack water when output falls to zero, and the tidal range varies with the spring/neap cycle.

factual_errors.text: Fossil fuels and nuclear can supply energy whenever it is needed.
factual_errors.correction: Nuclear power stations are reliable because they do not depend on the weather. However, they are slow to start up and cannot quickly change output to meet demand. The lesson's own table says nuclear is "slow to start". The same claim appears in checkpoints[2].correctFeedback: "A nuclear power station can supply energy whenever it is needed."

factual_errors.text: Renewables are FREE to run but INTERMITTENT.
factual_errors.correction: Not all renewables are free to run. Bio-fuel has fuel costs, and all renewables have maintenance costs. Hydroelectric, geothermal and bio-fuel are not intermittent. The lesson itself lists "Thinking renewable means 'free' or 'clean'" in commonMistakes[3].
Bio-fuel is a renewable resource because it can be replenished as it is used. The lesson's own keyTerms ("renewable energy ... bio-fuel") and revisionCardBullets also list it as renewable.

wrong_terms.text: For 'why high voltage in the grid' questions
The grid uses high voltage because cutting the current cuts cable losses by its square.
The I²R equation is the key to explaining WHY high voltage is used.
